title: Checkpoint: The Building Blocks
objective: After this level you can connect cells, DNA, tissues and organs into one picture of how a body is built.
summary: Systems, organs, tissues, cells, DNA: one zoom. About 330 billion cells are replaced daily, and each new cell comes from an old one with a full copy of the DNA.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: you're being rebuilt while you read this.
cards.body: Every second, millions of your cells are replaced. First, a quick zoom through everything this chapter built. Then, how the building blocks keep renewing themselves.

cards.headline: Zoom from you to a single gene
cards.body: Start with you: 11 organ systems. Zoom into the digestive system and pick one organ, the stomach, built from four tissue types. Zoom into a tissue: similar cells working together, part of about 30 trillion human cells. Open one cell and find the nucleus, holding 46 chromosomes of DNA. Read one gene, and a ribosome builds a protein from its message.

cards.fact: About 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day.
cards.context: That's roughly 1 percent of them, or about 3.8 million every second, according to a 2021 estimate by Ron Sender and Ron Milo. Blood leads the way: about 90 percent of the new cells are blood cells.

cards.headline: Every new cell gets the whole book
cards.body: New cells come only from existing cells, one of the rules of cell theory. When a cell divides, each new cell needs an exact copy of the old cell's DNA, and each of DNA's two strands serves as the pattern for a copy. So Level 5's instruction book is being copied all day long, and you never feel a thing.

mascot.line: Billions of copies a day, and hardly a typo that matters. Best printing press you will ever own.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: How your body is built in levels, from cells to tissues to organs to eleven teamed-up systems.
What a cell's membrane, nucleus and mitochondria each do to keep it running.
How a gene in your DNA becomes a working protein, through a messenger copy read by a ribosome.
Why you carry about as many bacteria as human cells, and how those microbes earn their keep.

questions.prompt: Building Blocks recap: about how many of your cells are replaced each day?

options.label: About 330 thousand
options.rationale: Far too few: that many go in well under a second.

questions.explanation: Sender and Milo estimated about 330 billion cells a day, roughly 1 percent of the body's cells.

questions.prompt: Building Blocks recap: why must a cell copy its DNA before it divides into two?

options.label: Each new cell needs its own exact copy
Old DNA wears out and is thrown away
options.rationale: The old strands serve as patterns for the copies.

options.label: DNA is food for the new cell
The copies replace the nucleus
options.rationale: The DNA is kept in the nucleus; it does not replace it.

questions.explanation: When a cell divides, each new cell needs an exact copy of the old cell's DNA.

questions.prompt: Building Blocks recap: which list zooms in from the largest level of the body to the smallest?

options.label: Organ, organ system, cell, tissue
options.rationale: Organ systems are bigger than organs.

options.label: Tissue, organ, organ system, cell
options.rationale: Organs are made of tissues, so tissues are smaller.

options.label: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system
options.rationale: That runs from smallest to largest.

questions.explanation: Organ systems are made of organs, organs of tissues, and tissues of cells.

questions.prompt: Building Blocks recap, from Level 7: why doesn't one 'percent water' figure fit everyone?

options.label: Water share is the same for all ages
options.rationale: It falls from about 75 percent at birth.

options.label: It changes with age and body fat
Only athletes contain water
options.rationale: Every body is about half water or more.

options.label: Water leaves the body at night
options.rationale: The share depends on age and tissue mix.

questions.explanation: Water is about 75 percent of a newborn and 50 to 60 percent of an adult, and more body fat means a lower share.

questions.prompt: Building Blocks recap, from Level 9: what did Robert Hooke name after looking at cork through a lens?

options.label: The gene
options.rationale: Genes come from a much later science.

options.label: The tissue
options.rationale: Hooke named the box-like units themselves.

questions.explanation: In Micrographia (1665), Robert Hooke coined the word "cell" for the box-like structures in cork.
